reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: A rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour secreting vasoactive intestinal peptide, producing the syndrome of watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, and achlorhydria
The diarrhoea is large-volume and secretory, meaning it persists during fasting, unlike osmotic diarrhoea
Profound potassium loss in stool causes hypokalaemia with weakness, and dehydration can be severe
VIP also tends to reduce gastric acid secretion (achlorhydria or hypochlorhydria) and may cause flushing and hypercalcaemia
Diagnosis relies on demonstrating a markedly elevated fasting plasma VIP level in the setting of secretory diarrhoea
Most tumours are located in the pancreas and a substantial proportion are malignant with metastases at diagnosis, so cross-sectional and functional imaging are needed for localisation and staging
Consider an association with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 in appropriate clinical contexts
Initial management prioritises aggressive rehydration and correction of electrolyte disturbance, with somatostatin analogues to control secretion and surgery for resectable disease
reference.pathophysiology: A VIPoma is a functioning neuroendocrine tumour, usually arising in the pancreatic islets, that secretes excessive vasoactive intestinal peptide. VIP stimulates intestinal secretion of water and electrolytes while inhibiting absorption, producing a high-volume secretory diarrhoea that continues despite fasting. The consequent losses of potassium and bicarbonate in stool lead to hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis, and VIP's inhibition of gastric acid secretion causes achlorhydria. VIP can also promote vasodilation and flushing and, through its effects on bone and calcium handling, contribute to hypercalcaemia. A significant proportion of these tumours are malignant and may have metastasised, most often to the liver, by the time of diagnosis.
additionalDifferentials: Other secretory diarrhoeas such as gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes, bicarbonate, calcium, and glucose to characterise the metabolic disturbance
Stool studies to confirm a secretory pattern and exclude other causes
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of the pancreas and liver for localisation and staging
Somatostatin-receptor functional imaging for occult or metastatic disease
Screening for other endocrine tumours where MEN1 is suspected
redFlags: Severe dehydration and haemodynamic instability from massive fluid loss
Metastatic disease, most commonly hepatic, at presentation
Refractory diarrhoea unresponsive to initial supportive measures
reference.prognosis: Symptom control with rehydration and somatostatin analogues is usually achievable, and complete surgical resection of localised disease can be curative; however, many tumours are malignant with metastases at diagnosis, and prognosis then depends on tumour burden and response to systemic therapy.
pitfalls: Attributing chronic watery diarrhoea to common causes and delaying measurement of VIP
Failing to recognise the secretory nature of the diarrhoea because it persists with fasting
Under-resuscitating profound fluid and potassium losses
Overlooking a possible MEN1 association and associated tumours
management: Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide or lanreotide to suppress vasoactive intestinal peptide secretion and control the secretory diarrhoea
Aggressive rehydration and correction of hypokalaemia, bicarbonate loss and metabolic acidosis in the acute setting
Surgical resection of localised tumour, which can be curative, with debulking for symptom control in advanced disease
Systemic and liver-directed therapy for metastatic disease, including peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, targeted agents such as everolimus or sunitinib, and hepatic embolisation
Monitor plasma VIP, electrolytes and cross-sectional and somatostatin-receptor imaging for treatment response and recurrence
Manage within a neuroendocrine tumour multidisciplinary team
Screen for MEN1 and offer genetic counselling where a familial endocrine syndrome is suspected
